topics.title: Advanced grammar: passive, subjunctive and punctuation
topics.intro: The grammar that makes writing sound sophisticated: the passive voice, the subjunctive mood, modal verbs, and the colon, semicolon and dash used with purpose.
topics.teach: Explain when a writer might choose the passive voice.
topics.talk: Challenge her to say three sentences in the passive at dinner (“The peas were eaten by…”).

topics.title: Ambitious vocabulary
topics.intro: Twelve words that top-set essays use and most eleven-year-olds do not. Learn them, then use each one in a real sentence this week.
topics.teach: Use three of this week’s words in one paragraph about your day.
topics.talk: Pick a word and see who can use it first, naturally, during the day.

topics.title: Spelling: words everyone gets wrong
topics.intro: Not on the Year 6 list, but these are the words that lose marks in Year 7 and 8: separate, definitely, occasionally, manoeuvre…
topics.teach: Pick one word and explain its trap.
topics.talk: Ask her to spell “definitely” and “separate” out loud.

topics.title: Poetic form: the sonnet and the ballad
topics.intro: Form is the shape of a poem: how many lines, what rhymes, what rhythm. Shakespeare’s Sonnet 18 is the most famous fourteen lines in English.
topics.talk: Clap the ten syllables of “Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day?” together.

topics.title: Reading: Dickens and Brontë
topics.intro: Two openings from great Victorian novels. The sentences are long and the vocabulary is hard. Slow down, reread, and trust the clues.
topics.teach: Explain how Dickens makes the convict frightening in a single paragraph.
topics.talk: Read the first paragraph of Great Expectations aloud together, as dramatically as you can.

items.prompt: Which sentence is in the passive voice?

options.text: The window was broken by the ball.
The ball broke the window.
options.feedback: Here the ball (the doer) is the subject: active voice.

options.text: The ball is breaking the window.
options.feedback: Still active: the doer is the subject, just in a different tense.

items.explain: In the passive, the thing the action is done TO becomes the subject (“The window was broken”). The doer can be added with “by” or left out.

items.prompt: Why might a scientist write “The liquid was heated to 80°C” instead of “I heated the liquid to 80°C”?

options.text: The passive keeps the focus on the experiment
Because scientists are never allowed to use “I”
options.feedback: There is no rule, but the passive is the convention because it focuses on the process.

options.text: Because the passive is shorter and quicker to write
options.feedback: It is actually longer. The reason is focus and formality.

items.explain: The passive is useful when the doer is unknown, unimportant, or when you want to hide them (“Mistakes were made”).

items.prompt: Rewrite in the passive: “The dog chased the cat.”
items.answer: The cat was chased by the dog.
distractors: The dog was chasing the cat.
items.explain: Object becomes subject (the cat), verb becomes “was chased”, doer goes after “by”.
accept: the cat was chased by the dog

items.prompt: “If I were you, I would apologise.” Why “were” and not “was”?

options.text: It is the subjunctive, for imagined situations
It is a mistake that should be “was”
options.feedback: It is correct formal English. “Were” after “if I” shows something imagined.

options.text: Because “I” counts as plural in this sentence
options.feedback: “I” is never plural. The form is the subjunctive.

items.explain: The subjunctive appears in formal wishes and demands too: “I wish it were Friday”; “The head insists that every pupil be on time.”

items.prompt: Which word in “You must finish, but you could ask for help” is NOT a modal verb?
items.explain: Modal verbs (can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will, would) show how certain, possible or necessary something is. “Finish” is an ordinary verb.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses the colon correctly?

options.text: She packed three things: a torch, a map and a sandwich.
She packed: a torch, a map and a sandwich.
options.feedback: A colon needs a complete sentence before it. “She packed” is not complete on its own.

options.text: She packed three things, a torch: a map and a sandwich.
options.feedback: The colon must come where the list is introduced.

items.explain: A colon says “here it comes”: it introduces a list, an explanation or an example after a complete sentence.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses the semicolon correctly?

options.text: The rain stopped; we went outside.
The rain stopped; and we went outside.
options.feedback: A semicolon replaces the joining word. Use one or the other.

options.text: Because the rain stopped; we went outside.
options.feedback: “Because the rain stopped” is not a complete sentence, so it cannot stand on one side of a semicolon.

items.explain: A semicolon joins two complete sentences that are closely related. Each side could stand alone.

items.prompt: “My brother – who never reads – finished the book in a day.” What job are the dashes doing?

options.text: Marking parenthesis: extra, removable information
Showing a pause for breath when reading aloud
options.feedback: They mark off an extra clause, like brackets or a pair of commas.

options.text: Joining two words into a compound
options.feedback: That is a hyphen (shorter, no spaces): “well-known”.

items.explain: Brackets, a pair of commas or a pair of dashes all mark parenthesis. Dashes are the most dramatic; brackets the quietest.

items.prompt: In “The book that I lost was a present”, what kind of clause is “that I lost”?

options.text: A relative clause describing “book”
A main clause that could stand alone
options.feedback: It cannot stand alone; it adds information about the book.

options.text: An adverbial clause saying when
options.feedback: Adverbial clauses tell you when, where, why or how. This one describes a noun.

items.explain: Relative clauses start with who, which, that, whose, where or when and work like adjectives.

items.prompt: Which version avoids the ambiguity: “a man eating shark” or “a man-eating shark”?
items.explain: Without the hyphen it could be a man who is eating shark. The hyphen joins “man-eating” into one adjective.

items.prompt: Which word means “extremely careful about every detail”?
items.explain: meticulous: extremely careful about every detail. “She kept a meticulous diary, recording even the weather.”
items.learn:
**meticulous**: extremely careful about every detail.
_She kept a meticulous diary, recording even the weather._

items.prompt: Which word means “having mixed feelings about something”?
items.explain: ambivalent: having mixed feelings about something. “He felt ambivalent about moving: excited and sad at once.”
items.learn:
**ambivalent**: having mixed feelings about something.
_He felt ambivalent about moving: excited and sad at once._

items.prompt: Which word means “lasting a very short time”?
items.explain: ephemeral: lasting a very short time. “Snowflakes are ephemeral; they melt as they land.”
items.learn:
**ephemeral**: lasting a very short time.
_Snowflakes are ephemeral; they melt as they land._

items.prompt: Which word means “dealing with things sensibly and practically”?
items.explain: pragmatic: dealing with things sensibly and practically. “A pragmatic captain picks the team that will win, not her friends.”
items.learn:
**pragmatic**: dealing with things sensibly and practically.
_A pragmatic captain picks the team that will win, not her friends._

items.prompt: Which word means “kind and generous”?
items.explain: benevolent: kind and generous. “The benevolent king gave grain to the poor every winter.”
items.learn:
**benevolent**: kind and generous.
_The benevolent king gave grain to the poor every winter._

items.prompt: Which word means “to examine very closely”?
items.explain: scrutinise: to examine very closely. “The referee scrutinised the replay before deciding.”
items.learn:
**scrutinise**: to examine very closely.
_The referee scrutinised the replay before deciding._

items.prompt: Which word means “refusing to give up”?
items.explain: tenacious: refusing to give up. “The tenacious climber tried the route for the fifth time.”
items.learn:
**tenacious**: refusing to give up.
_The tenacious climber tried the route for the fifth time._

items.prompt: Which word means “more than is needed; unnecessary”?
items.explain: superfluous: more than is needed; unnecessary. “Cut the superfluous words and the sentence gets stronger.”
items.learn:
**superfluous**: more than is needed; unnecessary.
_Cut the superfluous words and the sentence gets stronger._

items.prompt: Which word means “speaking or writing fluently and persuasively”?
items.explain: eloquent: speaking or writing fluently and persuasively. “Her eloquent speech won over the whole hall.”
items.learn:
**eloquent**: speaking or writing fluently and persuasively.
_Her eloquent speech won over the whole hall._

items.prompt: Which word means “found everywhere”?
items.explain: ubiquitous: found everywhere. “Mobile phones are now ubiquitous.”
items.learn:
**ubiquitous**: found everywhere.
_Mobile phones are now ubiquitous._

items.prompt: Which word means “truthful and straightforward, even when awkward”?
items.explain: candid: truthful and straightforward, even when awkward. “Be candid: did you like the film?”
items.learn:
**candid**: truthful and straightforward, even when awkward.
_Be candid: did you like the film?_

items.prompt: Which word means “certain to happen; unavoidable”?
items.explain: inevitable: certain to happen; unavoidable. “After weeks without rain, the hosepipe ban was inevitable.”
items.learn:
**inevitable**: certain to happen; unavoidable.
_After weeks without rain, the hosepipe ban was inevitable._

items.explain: There is “a rat” in sep-a-rat-e: two a’s, not an e in the middle.
items.learn: **separate**: There is “a rat” in sep-a-rat-e: two a’s, not an e in the middle.

items.explain: Built on “finite”: de-finite-ly. No “a” anywhere.
items.learn: **definitely**: Built on “finite”: de-finite-ly. No “a” anywhere.

items.explain: Double c, single s: oc-cas-ion-al-ly.
items.learn: **occasionally**: Double c, single s: oc-cas-ion-al-ly.

items.explain: in-depend-ence: ends -ence, like dependence.
items.learn: **independence**: in-depend-ence: ends -ence, like dependence.

items.explain: know + ledge: keep the silent k and the d.
items.learn: **knowledge**: know + ledge: keep the silent k and the d.

items.sentence: They had an ___ about the rules.
items.explain: Argue drops its e before -ment: argu-ment.
items.learn: **argument**: Argue drops its e before -ment: argu-ment.

items.explain: busi-ness: busy changes y to i, then -ness.
items.learn: **business**: busi-ness: busy changes y to i, then -ness.

items.sentence: My ___ at work lent me a pen.
items.explain: col-league: double l, then -eague.
items.learn: **colleague**: col-league: double l, then -eague.

items.explain: fa-sci-nat-ing: the sc makes one “s” sound.
items.learn: **fascinating**: fa-sci-nat-ing: the sc makes one “s” sound.

items.explain: Humour loses its u before -ous: hum-or-ous.
items.learn: **humorous**: Humour loses its u before -ous: hum-or-ous.

items.explain: A French word: man-oeu-vre. Say “man-oh-ee-u-vre” to remember the vowels.
items.learn: **manoeuvre**: A French word: man-oeu-vre. Say “man-oh-ee-u-vre” to remember the vowels.

items.explain: par-all-el: double l in the middle, single at the end.
items.learn: **parallel**: par-all-el: double l in the middle, single at the end.

items.explain: per-sever-ance: no “r” after the e (not perserverance).
items.learn: **perseverance**: per-sever-ance: no “r” after the e (not perserverance).

items.explain: question + naire: double n.
items.learn: **questionnaire**: question + naire: double n.

items.learn: **vacuum**: Double u, single c: vac-uum.

items.prompt: How many lines does a sonnet have?
items.explain: Fourteen lines: in Shakespeare’s sonnets, three quatrains (groups of four) and a final couplet.

items.prompt: “Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day?” has ten syllables with five beats: da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM. What is this rhythm called?

options.text: Iambic pentameter
Free verse
options.feedback: Free verse has no regular rhythm. This line is as regular as a heartbeat.

options.text: A couplet
options.feedback: A couplet is two rhyming lines, not a rhythm.

items.explain: Iamb = da-DUM; pentameter = five of them. Shakespeare’s plays are mostly written in it too.
items.passage:
Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day?
Thou art more lovely and more temperate:
Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May,
And summer’s lease hath all too short a date:
Sometime too hot the eye of heaven shines,
And often is his gold complexion dimm’d;
And every fair from fair sometime declines,
By chance or nature’s changing course untrimm’d;
But thy eternal summer shall not fade
Nor lose possession of that fair thou owest;
Nor shall Death brag thou wander’st in his shade,
When in eternal lines to time thou growest:
So long as men can breathe or eyes can see,
So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.

items.prompt: Look at the line endings: day/temperate/May/date… What is the rhyme scheme of the first four lines?

options.text: ABAB
AABB
options.feedback: Day does not rhyme with temperate. The rhymes alternate: day/May, temperate/date.

options.text: ABBA
options.feedback: Line 1 rhymes with line 3, not line 4.

items.explain: A Shakespearean sonnet runs ABAB CDCD EFEF GG: three quatrains and a couplet.

items.prompt: Line 9 begins “But thy eternal summer shall not fade”. What happens here?

options.text: The volta: a turn to the loved one’s lasting beauty
A second, separate sonnet begins at this line
options.feedback: It is the same poem. Sonnets often change direction at line 9.

options.text: The rhyme scheme breaks down completely
options.feedback: The rhyme continues (EFEF). It is the ARGUMENT that turns.

items.explain: The volta is the hinge of a sonnet. “But” signals it: everything before was the problem, everything after is the answer.

items.prompt: What does the final couplet claim?

options.text: The poem will keep the loved one alive
Summer will last for ever in England
options.feedback: The poem says the opposite: “summer’s lease hath all too short a date”.

options.text: The poet himself will live for ever
options.feedback: It is “this” (the poem) and “thee” (the loved one) who live, through the lines.

items.explain: “So long lives this, and this gives life to thee”: the poem is the eternal summer. Rather a confident ending, and it has turned out to be true.

items.prompt: In “the eye of heaven”, what is being personified?
items.explain: The sun is the eye of heaven, with a “gold complexion” that can be “dimm’d” by cloud.

items.prompt: Which form tells a story in four-line stanzas, often with the rhyme ABCB and a refrain?
items.explain: Ballads were sung before they were written down: simple stanzas, a strong beat, a tragic or heroic story.

items.prompt: A haiku has three lines with how many syllables?
items.explain: Seventeen syllables, usually about nature and a single moment.

items.prompt: When a sentence runs on past the end of a line without a pause, it is called…
items.explain: Enjambment carries the reader forward; a caesura is a pause inside a line.

items.prompt: The convict is described in three sentences that all begin “A man…” What is the effect of this repetition?

options.text: It builds him up piece by frightening piece
It makes him seem ordinary and harmless
options.feedback: Each sentence adds something worse: “iron on his leg”, “soaked in water”, “cut by flints”.

options.text: It shows that Pip already knows him
options.feedback: Pip has never seen him before.

items.explain: Three sentences, no main verb in two of them: Dickens freezes the moment so we see the man as the terrified child does.
items.passage:
(Pip, a small orphan, is alone in the churchyard on the marshes at dusk.)

“Hold your noise!” cried a terrible voice, as a man started up from among the graves at the side of the church porch. “Keep still, you little devil, or I’ll cut your throat!”

A fearful man, all in coarse gray, with a great iron on his leg. A man with no hat, and with broken shoes, and with an old rag tied round his head. A man who had been soaked in water, and smothered in mud, and lamed by stones, and cut by flints, and stung by nettles, and torn by briars; who limped, and shivered, and glared, and growled; and whose teeth chattered in his head as he seized me by the chin.

“Oh! Don’t cut my throat, sir,” I pleaded in terror. “Pray don’t do it, sir.”

“Tell us your name!” said the man. “Quick!”

“Pip, sir.”

“Once more,” said the man, staring at me. “Give it mouth!”

“Pip. Pip, sir.”

“Show us where you live,” said the man. “Pint out the place!”

I pointed to where our village lay, on the flat in-shore among the alder-trees and pollards, a mile or more from the church.

The man, after looking at me for a moment, turned me upside down, and emptied my pockets. There was nothing in them but a piece of bread. When the church came to itself,—for he was so sudden and strong that he made it go head over heels before me, and I saw the steeple under my feet,—when the church came to itself, I say, I was seated on a high tombstone, trembling while he ate the bread ravenously.

“You young dog,” said the man, licking his lips, “what fat cheeks you ha’ got.”

I believe they were fat, though I was at that time undersized for my years, and not strong.

“Darn me if I couldn’t eat em,” said the man, with a threatening shake of his head, “and if I han’t half a mind to’t!”

I earnestly expressed my hope that he wouldn’t, and held tighter to the tombstone on which he had put me; partly, to keep myself upon it; partly, to keep myself from crying.

items.prompt: “who limped, and shivered, and glared, and growled”. Which word tells you the man is suffering as well as frightening?

options.text: shivered
glared
options.feedback: Glared is threatening. Shivered shows he is cold and in pain.

options.text: growled
options.feedback: Growled makes him animal-like; shivered makes him pitiable.

items.explain: Dickens makes the convict terrifying and pitiable at once. “Shivered” and “lamed by stones” hint that he is a victim too.

items.prompt: What does the man do when Pip points out where he lives?

options.text: Turns him upside down
Lets him go home to his sister
options.feedback: He is only beginning. He tips Pip up and takes his bread.

options.text: Walks off towards the village

items.explain: “The man, after looking at me for a moment, turned me upside down, and emptied my pockets.” The world literally turns over for Pip.

items.prompt: “When the church came to itself,—for he was so sudden and strong that he made it go head over heels before me”. Why does Dickens say the CHURCH turned over?

options.text: Pip is upside down, so the church seems to turn
An earthquake shook the old church to its roots
options.feedback: It is Pip who is turned, not the building.

options.text: Dickens made a mistake in the sentence
options.feedback: It is deliberate: the child sees the steeple under his feet.

items.explain: Telling it from inside Pip’s dizzy head is both funny and frightening. We never leave the child’s point of view.

I pointed to where our village lay, on the flat in-shore among the alder-trees and pollards, a mile or more from the church.

The man, after looking at me for a moment, turned me upside down, and emptied my pockets. There was nothing in them but a piece of bread. When the church came to itself,—for he was so sudden and strong that he made it go head over heels before me, and I saw the steeple under my feet,—when the church came to itself, I say, I was seated on a high tombstone, trembling while he ate the bread ravenously.

“You young dog,” said the man, licking his lips, “what fat cheeks you ha’ got.”

I believe they were fat, though I was at that time undersized for my years, and not strong.

“Darn me if I couldn’t eat em,” said the man, with a threatening shake of his head, “and if I han’t half a mind to’t!”

I earnestly expressed my hope that he wouldn’t, and held tighter to the tombstone on which he had put me; partly, to keep myself upon it; partly, to keep myself from crying.

“Hold your noise!” cried a terrible voice, as a man started up from among the graves at the side of the church porch. “Keep still, you little devil, or I’ll cut your throat!”

items.prompt: How does Dickens make the convict both frightening and pitiable in this extract? Write a paragraph using at least two quotations.
hints: Point: frightening (his voice, his threats, how he treats Pip)
Point: pitiable (his state: soaked, lamed, cut, shivering)
Comment on the structure of the “A man…” paragraph
What the reader feels, and why both sides matter
items.model: Dickens makes the convict frightening first through his voice: “Hold your noise!” and “I’ll cut your throat!” are the first words we hear, and he soon turns Pip “upside down”. Yet the description that follows makes him pitiable. He has been “soaked in water, and smothered in mud, and lamed by stones, and cut by flints”, and he “shivered” as well as “glared”. The repeated “A man…” sentences pile up these details like injuries. The reader is terrified with Pip but also starts to feel sorry for the man, which matters because Pip will later owe him everything.

items.passage:
(Jane, an orphan of ten, lives with her aunt Mrs Reed and her cousins, who do not want her.)

There was no possibility of taking a walk that day. We had been wandering, indeed, in the leafless shrubbery an hour in the morning; but since dinner (Mrs. Reed, when there was no company, dined early) the cold winter wind had brought with it clouds so sombre, and a rain so penetrating, that further out-door exercise was now out of the question.

I was glad of it: I never liked long walks, especially on chilly afternoons: dreadful to me was the coming home in the raw twilight, with nipped fingers and toes, and a heart saddened by the chidings of Bessie, the nurse, and humbled by the consciousness of my physical inferiority to Eliza, John, and Georgiana Reed.

The said Eliza, John, and Georgiana were now clustered round their mama in the drawing-room: she lay reclined on a sofa by the fireside, and with her darlings about her (for the time neither quarrelling nor crying) looked perfectly happy. Me, she had dispensed from joining the group; saying, “She regretted to be under the necessity of keeping me at a distance; but that until she heard from Bessie, and could discover by her own observation, that I was endeavouring in good earnest to acquire a more sociable and childlike disposition, a more attractive and sprightly manner—something lighter, franker, more natural, as it were—she really must exclude me from privileges intended only for contented, happy, little children.”

“What does Bessie say I have done?” I asked.

“Jane, I don’t like cavillers or questioners; besides, there is something truly forbidding in a child taking up her elders in that manner. Be seated somewhere; and until you can speak pleasantly, remain silent.”

A breakfast-room adjoined the drawing-room, I slipped in there. It contained a bookcase: I soon possessed myself of a volume, taking care that it should be one stored with pictures. I mounted into the window- seat: gathering up my feet, I sat cross-legged, like a Turk; and, having drawn the red moreen curtain nearly close, I was shrined in double retirement.

items.prompt: Mrs Reed says Jane needs “a more sociable and childlike disposition… something lighter, franker, more natural”. What does this reveal about Mrs Reed?

options.text: She blames Jane for being unhappy

items.prompt: How does Charlotte Brontë make the reader sympathise with Jane in this opening? Write a paragraph using at least two quotations.
hints: How Jane is treated (Mrs Reed’s words, the cousins “clustered round their mama”)
Jane’s own feelings and her refuge
The weather, and what it reflects
items.model: Brontë makes us sympathise with Jane by showing her shut out of her own family. The cousins are “clustered round their mama” while Jane is “dispensed from joining the group”, and Mrs Reed calls her a “caviller” for asking one question. Because Jane tells the story herself, we feel her “heart saddened by the chidings of Bessie” from the inside. The “drear November day” and “rain so penetrating” reflect her loneliness, and her hiding place, “shrined in double retirement”, shows a child making the only safe space she can.
